The current limits include files below 2 MiB, 100 saved workflows, 32 charts per workflow and 64 calculations. Imported definitions cannot supply executable Python or JavaScript. Resolve incompatibility Required source columns must exist with compatible types. A workflow built around a confidence column cannot be applied to a table with no confidence measurements. Inspect the error, supply the correct metrics or select the intended source, then retry. Failed application validates before replacing the current view. A calculation error may also reveal that a source column was renamed or removed. Preserve a working export before revising a complex setup. Analysis versus data selection A workflow describes a question; its answer changes with the rows loaded. If another person must use exactly the same samples for training, share the dataset version too. The built-in Evaluation and comparison screens provide specialised analysis. A managed catalogue of executable workflow plugins is Not yet included .

title: Explore embedding space
summary: Collect feature vectors and project them into a shared two- or three-dimensional coordinate system.
text: An embedding is a numeric description of a sample produced by a model or feature extractor. Nearby points can suggest similar samples, but the relationship depends on the model and preprocessing. Use the original images and labels to interpret a cluster. Collect vectors Use embedding collectors with your model, or the image similarity workflow for its available descriptors. Store vector columns with a fixed-size EmbeddingSchema ; ragged vectors, missing values or non-finite components cannot be projected. Keep the model, layer and preprocessing with the experiment so another run can reproduce them. Create a projection Save pending edits and open a table or run containing an embedding column. Choose Embeddings , then the vector column and projection method. Select two or three dimensions. Set neighbours and seed where applicable. Optionally choose Save this coordinate system for reuse and name it. Start the job, inspect its result, then choose Open projection . PCA is included with the core numeric dependencies. UMAP and PaCMAP require the reduction extra. A table projection creates a new dataset revision; a run projection creates a separate analysis run. For run data, a new fit uses the last available embedding table and transforms the other epochs through that coordinate system. Reuse a coordinate system Choose a saved projection when comparing another dataset or run. Use the same embedding model, layer and preprocessing. The service checks vector width; equal width does not prove two models produce compatible representations. Fitting each dataset independently makes axes incomparable. Python users can use Reducer , reduce_table and reduce_run from granum.reduction . Saved nonlinear reducers require trusted loading; see storage . Interpret carefully Projection compresses information. A gap in a 2D chart is not itself evidence of a bad label, and movement in a projection differs from distance in the full embedding space. Check several samples, then use duplicates , trajectories or a review queue to investigate. Large runs and additional GPU/browser combinations still require workload-specific qualification.

title: Follow samples across epochs
summary: Connect repeated observations and measure changes without losing sample identity.
text: A trajectory links measurements of the same sample through an ordered sequence. It can reveal unstable predictions, changing embeddings or examples that a model learns and later forgets. Collect more than one observation per sample before using this view. Prepare the observations Record per-sample metrics with an epoch or another numeric iteration column. Preserve each metrics row's input table reference and sample ID. A row number after sorting is not a stable identity across datasets. If the input revision changes, keep that change explicit rather than silently joining it to an earlier sample position. Draw a path Open the run workspace and create a scatter using two or three numerical axes. Configure the trajectory's grouping field and numeric order field. Use the identity representing one sample and order by epoch. Filter to a manageable selection and inspect a few paths against their image observations before interpreting the whole chart. Embedding trajectories should share a fitted projection . Independently fitting each epoch can rotate or rearrange the chart and create apparent movement unrelated to changes in the model representation. Measure full-vector travel With a vector embedding column, create a Previous observation calculation grouped by source and sample identity, ordered by epoch. Then calculate Euclidean distance between the current and previous vectors. Sum those distances within the same identity groups. The first observation has no previous vector and therefore no step distance. This produces travel in the original vector space. Chart distance in a reduced projection answers a different question. Different sampling intervals and numbers of recorded epochs also affect the summed distance. What remains reserved A guided, arbitrary N-column travel-distance wizard and component-comparison plot are Not yet included . See advanced analysis . Existing vector calculations and trajectory charts can be saved as analysis workflows . Treat unusually long paths as a review priority, not an automatic instruction to remove an image or increase its weight. Use sample learning and the source labels as supporting evidence.

title: Find duplicates leakage and outliers
summary: Review near-identical pictures, split leakage and unusual samples before trusting an evaluation.
text: Open Images → Duplicates to examine redundancy and related images across splits. Granum builds image descriptors and a neighbour graph. With training support it can use a learned descriptor; otherwise a colour-and-edge descriptor is a more limited signal. Read the descriptor shown by the result before interpreting similarity. Run the inspection Choose the dataset and ask Granum to read the images if descriptors are not present. Inspect Repeats for groups that may represent the same picture. Inspect Exported copies for known augmentation families and copies split across sets. Inspect Leaks for related pictures in training and evaluation. Inspect Outliers for samples with few close neighbours. Granum uses available provenance to distinguish an exported or augmented copy from a separately captured picture. Keep source names and augmentation metadata during conversion so this evidence survives. Similarity alone cannot always make that distinction. Make a decision Open representative images in a group. A sequence of similar frames can be a useful continuum, and a rare outlier can be exactly the case your model must learn. Select the specific images to move or remove only after checking their role in the task. Removal uses the same recoverable curation path as the rest of Images. Review the selection, confirm the action, then check Removed if you need to restore it. Create a new dataset version before training so the selection is recorded. Find neighbours of one image Use Find images like this from an image to order neighbours around that example. Existing split and metadata filters can narrow the result. Order by → Uniqueness ranks unusual images for inspection; a high score is a prompt to look, not a quality verdict. Check the consequence Revisit Health and split counts after curation. Hold related captures together when redesigning splits. Once training has seen an evaluation image or a close copy, simply removing that evaluation row cannot erase the information already learned by the model; design the next baseline on the corrected split.

title: Check dataset health
summary: Combine import, duplication, annotation and review evidence before creating a training version.
text: Health gathers the checks that already exist around a dataset into a readiness view. It helps you choose the next action before training, while the linked screens provide the evidence and editing tools needed to resolve it. Read the status A blocking result means a basic condition needs correction, such as an unusable split. A warning asks for investigation, such as excessive copies, rare classes, unreviewed model drafts or labels flagged by a model. An OK result means that particular check passed under its stated rule. Read the threshold and evidence behind each row. A result based on an import is different from one that requires embeddings or a completed model check. A check that has not run cannot establish the quality of the dataset. Work through a dataset Finish import and read its preflight report . Run the duplicate and leakage inspection when appropriate. Check class and object distributions in Images, including validation and test separately. Review model-drafted annotations and investigate Findings . Return to Health, follow unresolved checks and confirm the intended split membership. Create a named dataset version and record the reason for the selection. Health and approval Health is an operational summary. Approval is a separate gate over exact contents and matching review evidence. Passing a health threshold does not approve a version, and approving a version does not prove that every label is objectively correct. Use the project's intended criteria when deciding which warnings are acceptable. A deliberately rare class may need more representative data rather than removal; a model's weak recall can explain many findings without proving that the labels are wrong. When results change New imports, label edits, moved images and new model measurements can change the conclusion. Recheck the evidence before approving a newly created version or comparing it with an earlier baseline. Keep the earlier version and run so the change remains traceable through comparison .

title: Inspect model errors
summary: Read confusion, per-class results, operating thresholds and the individual objects behind each metric.
text: Open Evaluation for a run with stored predictions. Start with the evaluation dataset version and epoch, then inspect errors by class and object. An aggregate score alone does not identify the labels or failure modes worth working on. Read the confusion view The detection confusion matrix pairs overlapping labels and predictions without first requiring the same class. This makes a class mix-up visible in one cell. Select a cell to inspect the objects behind it, comparing the stored label with the predicted geometry. Class-aware scoring treats that same wrong-class prediction as a false positive and the unmatched label as a false negative. These are two useful interpretations of the same observation; do not expect their object counts to be identical to a class-agnostic confusion cell. Inspect class performance Read precision, recall, F1, support and available average-precision measurements per class. A class with very few labelled examples needs a different interpretation from a well-represented class. Inspect its images before using a small difference to choose a model. The threshold view shows how precision and recall change with confidence. Choose an operating point based on the task's costs and a held-out evaluation; a suggested best F1 threshold is not universally the best deployment threshold. Review the objects Use the found, invented and missed filters to inspect crops. A supposed false positive may expose a missing source label; a supposed miss may reveal an ambiguous or very small object. Open the source image to check the context and record a review decision . Changes to labels belong in a new revision. Keep the previous run's evaluation context and perform a new evaluation when you need scores against the corrected labels. Use Compare runs to check compatibility before drawing a before/after conclusion. Task boundaries Granum has task-specific overlap and keypoint metrics, and a Python semantic-mask collector. The specialised detection views do not make every task-specific evaluation dashboard available. New classification and semantic training paths are described in training tasks . Inspect their recorded metrics in the run workspace; a complete set of specialised evaluation screens for every task is Not yet included .

title: Review and verify
summary: Work through a dataset image by image or in bulk, with comments, rework and a progress bar.
headings: Working one image at a time
text: Review is a mode of the Images screen, not a separate place: turn on Review in the ribbon and the same grid becomes selectable, with a review bar above it and a decision tray below. Set up Type your name in the Reviewer box. It is remembered in this browser and attached to every decision and comment you make. There is no login; the name is a record among colleagues, not a credential. Working in bulk Tick images and act on all of them at once. Shift -click selects a range. Select shown takes the images loaded on the page; Select all takes everything matching the current filters, including images not yet loaded. The tray offers: Decision What it does Verify The labels are right Unverify Back to unverified, e.g. after fixing something Rework… Asks for a note saying what is wrong, and records it Isolate… Sets the images aside, out of new dataset versions, until returned Return to set Puts isolated images back where they came from Delete… Moves them to the removed set, recoverable The progress bar counts verified images against the total for the current filters, so the number moves as you work. Working one image at a time Click an image to open the inspector: the picture with its boxes on the left, the decision buttons, class counts and the comment thread on the right. Key Action ← → Previous / next image, saving any box edits first A Verify and move to the next image R Rework — write the reason in the comment box first U Back to unverified I Isolate B Show or hide boxes Delete Delete the selected box Ctrl + S Save box edits Ctrl + Enter Post the comment Esc Deselect the box, then close Boxes can be fixed here: drag on the image to draw one, click to select, Delete to remove. Anything more — moving, resizing, masks, keypoints, new classes — belongs in the editor , which the inspector links to. The rework loop Rework is how a reviewer hands an image back without losing the thread: The reviewer marks the image Rework with a note: "two pedestrians at the crossing are unlabelled" . The annotator filters to rework, reads the note, fixes the boxes, replies "added both" , and the image returns to unverified . The reviewer checks it again and verifies. Every step is appended to the image's thread with a name and a time, and nothing is overwritten, so the history of an image is always readable. How much to review You do not have to review everything before training, and usually should not. A sensible first pass: Verify the validation set properly. Every conclusion you draw later rests on it. Skim the training set for convention breaks rather than checking each image. Train, then let Findings tell you where in the training set to spend the rest of the effort. That ordering matters: reviewing 11,000 training images by hand before the first run is weeks of work, and the model can tell you which few hundred of them are worth your time.

title: Edit annotations
summary: Draw, move, relabel and delete boxes, masks and keypoints — and what each save writes.
text: Turn on Edit in the Images ribbon and open an image. The editor fills the screen: the image with its objects, a toolbar, and a panel with the selected object's class and properties. Tools Which tools appear follows the project's type . Tool Key What it does Select V Click an object to select it. Drag it to move, drag a handle to resize, drag a vertex or keypoint to move that point Box B Drag on the image to draw a box Oriented box O Draw a rectangle and use its rotation handle Polygon P Click points to trace a mask; Enter closes it. Double-click an edge to add a vertex Paint M Add pixels to the selected mask Erase E Remove pixels from the selected mask Keypoint K Click to add points to the selected object; with nothing selected, starts a new one Image label — For classification projects: one label for the whole image Detection projects get Box. Oriented detection adds rotated rectangles. Segmentation projects provide polygon and pixel tools, with SAM assistance when its dependencies are available. Keypoint projects get Keypoint, and a box is fitted around the points automatically when the project has no box tool. Classification projects get no drawing tools at all, only the image label. See boxes , masks and keypoints for the coordinate, export and task-specific rules. Moving around Action How Zoom Wheel Pan Drag empty space Fit the image 0 Previous / next image ← → — saves first Undo / redo Ctrl + Z / Ctrl + Shift + Z (or Ctrl + Y ) Save Ctrl + S , and automatically when you leave the image Delete Delete removes the picked vertex or keypoint, otherwise the whole object Classes The selected object's class is in the side panel; pick another to relabel it. + Class adds a new class to the dataset — available immediately on every set in it, because the class list belongs to the dataset rather than to one image. A class that is still in use cannot be removed, which is deliberate: silently dropping a class would change the meaning of every box that referred to it. Crowd and ignore regions Each object has a crowd toggle. A crowd object — COCO's iscrowd , or an "ignored region" in aerial datasets — is neither rewarded nor penalised: it is never matched, never counted as missed, and predictions lying mostly inside it are ignored rather than counted as false positives. Use it for regions you have deliberately not labelled individually. Getting this wrong is a common source of mysteriously bad precision: a dense crowd exported as one ordinary box means every correct person the model finds inside it counts against it. What a save writes One save writes one new version of that set , however many objects you changed, and sets the image back to unverified with a note saying what changed. The previous version is untouched. That is why the editor saves per image rather than per box: a session correcting forty images writes forty versions, not four hundred. If you are making a large sweep of edits, expect the version list to grow; it is the record of who changed what. Unsaved work is recoverable Both primary image editors keep acknowledged recovery copies in IndexedDB, in the same browser profile and origin. Clearing site data, quota failures or a crash before acknowledgement can lose drafts. A stale base disables automatic replay; export and reconcile against the latest revision. Failed server saves retain the draft. Browser recovery is not a server backup or cross-device sync. Follow the recorded recovery exercise for exact actions, the real dialog, screenshots and a captioned video. That exercise restores its practice relabel before saving; it does not manufacture a source-label correction.

title: Bounding boxes and rotated boxes
summary: Import, edit and measure ordinary detection boxes and oriented object annotations.
text: Boxes identify object extent and class within an image. Ordinary boxes align with image axes; oriented boxes retain four rotated corners. Choose the task before import so coordinate interpretation, editing tools and evaluation agree. Ordinary detection boxes A stored geometry value has image width , height and an instances list. Each ordinary box uses vertices: [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max] in source-image pixels and a numeric label . COCO's [x, y, width, height] and YOLO's normalised coordinates are converted by the importers. Import a COCO or YOLO detection dataset. Open Images → Edit and select an image. Choose Box to draw, or Select to move and resize an existing object. Check the selected class, crowd flag and any draft provenance. Save, then review the image again. Editing invalidates review evidence for the changed contents. granum.BoundingBoxes2D , box_iou , match_boxes and nms support Python detection workflows. Custom instance properties must be declared in the schema; see schemas . Oriented boxes Use the oriented-box task and a YOLO OBB dataset. The editor supports creating and adjusting rotated rectangles, including rotation and resizing within image bounds. Inspect all four corners after a change, especially near the edge of an image. The enclosing axis-aligned rectangle alone does not retain the object's orientation. Export using export_yolo(..., task="obb") . Out-of-range normalised coordinates are rejected. The YOLO adapter and task-aware metrics use rotated overlap for OBB matching. A detector evaluated with ordinary enclosing-box overlap answers a different question. Measure and export Use Evaluation to inspect true positives, false positives and missed labels. A class disagreement may appear differently in a confusion matrix and in class-aware scoring. For a round trip, export a small version and import it into a separate project; compare class maps, image references and geometry before exporting the entire collection. Three-dimensional cuboids are Not yet included ; see spatial data .

title: Instance and semantic masks
summary: Import mask labels, correct pixels and choose an export that preserves the information you need.
text: Instance segmentation gives each object its own mask. Semantic segmentation assigns each pixel a class, with an optional ignore value. Treat these as different tasks even when both are drawn as coloured overlays. Import masks COCO supports polygon and run-length encoded instance masks. YOLO segmentation uses polygons. Native semantic import uses lossless PNG masks and a semantic.json manifest. This minimal manifest names one image, its mask and the class IDs stored in that mask: { "format": "granum-semantic-masks", "version": 1, "ignore_index": 255, "categories": [{"id": 0, "name": "background"}, {"id": 1, "name": "part"}], "images": [{"file_name": "images/sample.png", "mask": "masks/sample.png"}] } Paths resolve relative to the manifest unless an explicit image root is supplied. Mask dimensions must match the source image. Class IDs and the ignore value must be distinct, valid integers; RGB mask inputs need an explicit colour mapping. See the Python API . Correct a mask Open an image in Edit mode and select the intended object or semantic class. Use Polygon for outlines, Paint for pixel additions, and Erase for pixel removal. Adjust brush diameter and inspect boundaries at a useful zoom level. In semantic work, confirm that painting one class has not left overlapping class regions. Save and reopen the image to verify the stored result. Re-review the changed image. SAM assistance can propose a mask from points or a box. Inspect the proposal before applying it; it remains a model suggestion until reviewed. Export and measure COCO RLE and native semantic PNGs preserve exact mask pixels. YOLO polygon conversion can change fine edges, holes or disconnected shapes. Semantic PNG export rejects conflicting class overlaps and writes the class/ignore metadata with the masks. Instance metrics use mask IoU. SemanticMetricsCollector accepts original-resolution class-ID maps and records pixel accuracy, per-class intersections/unions and IoU. Ignored pixels do not contribute; a class absent from the relevant data has no IoU, rather than a perfect one. Training boundary YOLO instance-segmentation training and prediction collection are included. The development branch also includes a Torchvision LR-ASPP semantic-training path, with broader workflow qualification still in progress. Follow training tasks for its input requirements. Connect other semantic architectures through the custom metrics contract .

title: Keypoints and pose
summary: Preserve landmark order, visibility and identity through import, editing, augmentation and evaluation.
text: Keypoints describe named positions on an object. Their order is part of the label contract: left eye and right eye must keep the same meaning through data loading, horizontal flips and prediction. Import and inspect Use COCO keypoints or Table.from_yolo_url(..., task="pose") . Keep skeleton definitions, keypoint names, visibility and any left/right flip mapping with the dataset. A model expecting a different number or order of points cannot be compared directly with those labels. Open Images in Edit mode. Select the object, use the Keypoint tool to add or adjust points, and check the selected point's visibility. An unlabelled point is different from an occluded point with a known position. Clearing a landmark must retain the layout expected by the model. Analyse individual landmarks In a table or run workspace containing keypoint metadata, open Landmarks . Choose the landmark slot and inspect its observations. Per-object properties such as keypoint_0_oks and keypoint_0_confidence can be used in numeric filters and charts when predictions were collected. A missing score is not zero. Unlabelled ground-truth landmarks have no score; filtering to a low score must not silently include them as failures. Mixed class-specific landmark layouts require care when interpreting a slot index. Automatic name display across all mixed layouts remains Not yet included . Train and export YOLO pose training, predictions and export use task="pose" . Matching uses Object Keypoint Similarity (OKS), with object scale and the supplied keypoint tolerance configuration. Inspect the prediction coordinate frame before comparing it to the original image. Horizontal pose augmentation requires declared flip_idx metadata to swap left/right landmarks. If it is absent, do not enable that transform as though it preserved labels. Start with one example, inspect every transformed point, then create the augmented dataset version . Export a small pose dataset and reimport it to check landmark count, class mapping and visibility. Sample metrics and Ultralytics integration explain how to attach observations to the right images across epochs.

title: Draft labels with a model
summary: Generate annotation suggestions, preserve their provenance and review them before approving a dataset.
text: Pre-labelling turns a model's predictions into draft annotations for human correction. Use it to reduce repetitive drawing when the model understands the classes you need. A confident prediction is still a suggestion. Prepare the request Open Images → Pre-label and choose the sets to process. Select a compatible project model or a supported pretrained model. Check the task and class mapping: a general pretrained model may know only some of your dataset's classes. Choose the confidence threshold based on the amount of correction you can review. A higher threshold usually creates fewer suggestions but can omit real objects. A lower threshold creates more drafts that may need deletion. Choose what may change Leave them alone preserves already labelled images and drafts labels on empty ones. Redraw them replaces existing annotations with the model's proposals in the new version. Read this choice before starting a large job. The job writes new set revisions. Source revisions remain available. Draft annotations carry their source and confidence where supported; existing manual annotations retain their distinct provenance. The dashboard marks draft geometry so it can be distinguished during review. Review and save Wait for job completion and inspect any reported errors or unsupported classes. Open a representative mix of easy, crowded, small-object and empty images. Correct classes, geometry and missing objects in the editor. Save each change and record the human review result. Check draft counts and Health before creating a dataset version. If results are unsuitable, continue from the earlier revision rather than treating the draft as verified data. Findings can help prioritise disagreements but do not replace the review. Preconditions The model environment and weights must be available to the service. Another model job may occupy the worker; finish or cancel it before starting a conflicting request. Use SAM for interactive mask proposals. Fully automatic dataset-wide segmentation and an active-labelling scheduler are Not yet included .

title: Propose masks with SAM
summary: Guide segmentation with points or an object box, then inspect and apply the proposed mask.
text: SAM assistance creates a mask proposal for the image you are editing. It needs training support with PyTorch and Ultralytics, plus the selected model's weights. A proposal does not become a saved annotation until you apply it and save the edit. Make a proposal Open a segmentation image in Edit mode and select the object or class you intend to change. Choose a model in the SAM panel. The catalogue includes MobileSAM and SAM 2.1 variants. Provide a bounding box or foreground point. Add background points where you need to exclude pixels. Choose Propose mask and wait for the job to complete. Inspect the overlay, especially holes, touching objects and fine boundaries. Apply a satisfactory proposal, refine it with Paint or Erase if needed, then save the image. Prompt coordinates must lie within the original image. The interactive service accepts up to 128 points and images with known dimensions up to 25 million pixels. It checks that the selected image belongs to the requested table and dataset. Change a proposal If the mask is wrong, adjust prompts and generate another proposal. Do not apply an old result to a different object or changed prompt set. Keep the model job's error or status visible until you know whether it completed; inspect the job log if weights, dependencies or resources are unavailable. For semantic labels, check class exclusivity after applying a mask. A pixel must not end up assigned to conflicting classes. The editor's task behaviour matters when replacing or merging a proposal. Save and review A confirmed editor save creates a new revision and invalidates review evidence for changed contents. Reopen the image and confirm the stored mask before marking it reviewed. Browser recovery helps with unfinished edits, but the saved revision is the durable result; follow any recovery warning shown by the editor. MobileSAM and SAM 2.1 tiny have development CPU inference evidence. Larger variants, GPUs and your image sizes need their own qualification. Dataset-wide automatic SAM labelling and a dedicated SAM embedding recipe are Not yet included ; see planned compute .

title: Control sample weights
summary: Exclude or emphasise training samples while preserving the underlying dataset and evaluation rules.
text: A sample weight records how strongly an input should participate in sampling. Granum normally adds a weight column initialised to 1. A zero weight excludes the sample from Granum samplers that honour weights; the source row can still exist in the table. Change weights as a revision from granum import Table table = Table.from_names("inspection", "train", "initial") weighted = table.set_weights({0: 0.0, 2: 2.0}) print(weighted.url) This example excludes row 0 and emphasises row 2 in a new version. Replace the names and indices with the dataset you inspected. Pin the resulting URL when you want training to use that exact choice. Use the workspace's editable weight column when reviewing samples visually. Save changes and inspect the resulting revision. Exclusion by weight, recoverable removal and permanent deletion have different consequences; choose the operation that matches your intent. Choose a sampler Sampler Meaning create_weighted_sampler Draw proportional to positive weight create_random_sampler Shuffle nonzero-weight samples once create_sequential_sampler Visit nonzero-weight samples in order create_repeat_by_weight_sampler Repeat according to the integer weight convention Pass the sampler to a PyTorch DataLoader and do not also request DataLoader shuffling. Merely storing a weight column does not force an arbitrary external training framework to use it. Verify the actual sampler or exporter used by your recipe. Keep evaluation interpretable Metrics collection includes zero-weight rows by default. Pass exclude_zero_weights=True only when that is the evaluation population you intend, and record the choice. Changing validation weights or membership can make two run scores incomparable. A large loss or long embedding trajectory can justify review, but it is not automatically a reason to increase weight. Label errors can receive more training emphasis too. Inspect the sample, change one factor deliberately, and use comparison to evaluate the result. Automatic optimised coreset selection is Not yet included .

title: Isolate, remove and restore
summary: Set images aside, take them out of a set, and put them back.
text: Two different problems, two different answers. Isolate: not now Isolating moves images into the dataset's isolated set. Use it when a few images are blocking you — a client has to decide whether a reflection counts as a person, an image may be a privacy problem, a frame is too ambiguous to label today. Isolated images stay out of new dataset versions, so the rest of the work continues. They keep their status, comments and labels, and can still be reviewed and edited. They appear as an isolated chip beside the splits in the Images ribbon. Return to set puts each back into the newest version of the set it came from. Isolating and returning each write a new version of the sets involved. Delete: not this Deleting moves images into the dataset's removed set, after a confirmation, with an optional reason. They leave the working sets and every future version. Nothing is destroyed. The file on disk is not touched, earlier versions still contain the image, and the removed set records where each image came from and why. Use it for images that should not be in the dataset at all: duplicates, corrupt files, photographs from the wrong site, images a customer has asked you to drop. Restoring The Removed button in the Images header opens the removed set: each image with the set it came from, the reason, and when. Select images and Restore to put them back into the newest version of their original set. They return unverified. Which to use Situation Use Waiting on a decision Isolate Genuinely ambiguous, may come back Isolate Duplicate, corrupt, wrong dataset Delete Customer asked for removal Delete Image is fine but the labels are wrong Neither — fix the labels Removing images changes row positions Both operations write a new version in which rows have moved. Per-image metrics from an earlier run stay attached to the version they were collected on — Granum will not join them forward across a row change. Your existing runs keep working and keep showing the right images; they simply show the data as it was. → Image identity

title: Create a dataset version
summary: Freeze what you agreed on into the named dataset that training uses.
text: Create dataset in the Images header turns the sets you have been working on into a named, frozen dataset version. Training offers these and nothing else. The dialog Name and description. Give it something a colleague could act on: "v2 — crossing pedestrians added, ignore regions fixed" . Names must be unique within the dataset. The set table shows each set with its images, how many are verified and how many are not. This is the honest summary of what you are about to freeze. If anything is unverified , Granum says how many and asks which you want: Choice What is stored Use it when Use entire dataset A reference to the current version of each set You want everything; the unverified count is recorded and shown Use only verified Frozen copies of each set holding only its verified images You want a clean training set while review continues Only-verified mode writes new, frozen sets rather than filtering at training time, so the version is a fixed list of images that cannot change afterwards. Augmentation is offered next: No, or Yes with a recipe and a number of copies. → Augmentation Creating a plain version is instant. With augmentation it runs as a job — the images have to be generated — and you can watch or leave it. What is recorded Per set: the exact version, the image count and the verified count. Overall: the name, the description, who made it, when, the mode, and the augmentation recipe if any. Version numbers count every version ever made, so a deleted number is never reused. Isolated images are never included. Removed images are never included. On the Datasets screen Each version is a panel with its sets, an image strip, the split facts, and a Train button that opens the train dialog with that version already chosen. The sidebar badge counts them. Deleting a version The trash button shows what the version costs on disk and which runs used it, then removes its frozen files. Runs that used it keep their scores and their record of which version they used — they simply no longer have the images to hand. A version in use by a running training job cannot be deleted. Name versions after what changed, not when "v3" tells a colleague nothing in six weeks. "v3 — removed night frames, fixed ignore regions" is a sentence they can act on, and it is what the comparison report will print beside the numbers.

title: Augmentation
summary: Generate augmented copies into a dataset version, and see exactly what the model will see.
text: Granum augments by generating images into the dataset version , not by transforming batches during training. That costs disk and a few minutes; it buys two things: you can look at exactly what the model will be trained on, image by image; a run's input is a fixed set of files rather than a recipe plus a seed, so two runs on the same version saw the same pictures. Only the train set is augmented. Validation and test sets are left alone, because augmenting what you measure with makes the measurement meaningless. Building a recipe In the Create dataset dialog, choose Yes , then how many augmented copies of each image to make (1–5×). Below that is a grid of cards, one per operation, each showing that operation applied to a real image from your own train set. Click a card to open its settings: the original, the minimum and the maximum of the range, with the controls between them. Add puts it in the recipe. Group Operations Geometry Flip (horizontal, vertical), 90° rotate, Crop, Rotation, Shear Colour and noise Grayscale, Hue, Saturation, Brightness, Exposure, Blur, Noise, Cutout Each copy draws each operation's value independently within its range, so a recipe of ±15° rotation and ±20% brightness gives copies that vary in both. What happens to the labels Geometric operations are composed into a single transform and applied to the image and to everything on it — boxes, mask polygons and keypoints together — so annotations stay attached to the pixels they describe. Two rules are worth knowing before you pick a range: Boxes that end up less than 15% visible are dropped. Heavy crops and large rotations therefore remove objects at the edges. The dataset version records how many were dropped, per set. Run-length masks cannot be transformed and are dropped under geometry. Polygon masks are transformed and clipped normally. Flips and left/right keypoints A horizontal flip mirrors keypoints but does not rename them, so a "left wrist" stays "left wrist" on what is now the right side. For keypoint projects with sided names, avoid horizontal flip until Granum swaps the pairs. The dialog says so where it matters. What it costs The dialog estimates the disk the generated images will take before you commit. As a rough guide, 2× copies of an 11,000-image set is 22,000 new JPEGs — a few gigabytes. The version records, per set, how many originals, how many augmented copies, and how many boxes and masks were dropped, and the Datasets screen shows the recipe, so nobody has to guess later what "v3 — augmented" contained. When to use it Augmentation is a way to make a small dataset go further, not a fix for a bad one. If Findings says 200 of your labels are wrong, augmenting produces five copies of each wrong label. Fix the data first, then augment the version you trust.

title: Export a dataset version
summary: Choose a target annotation format and media strategy, then verify the exported data.
text: Export a frozen dataset version when handing data to another tool or team. This keeps the export tied to the same revisions even if labels are edited later in the working dataset. Export from Datasets Open the intended dataset version and choose Export . Select the format and task variant supported by the receiving tool. Choose how image files should be included. Start the export and inspect the reported destination and outcome. Open the result in the receiving tool or reimport a small selection into a separate project. The normal destination is under the project's exports folder. Check available disk space when copying images. An export writes dataset files; it is not a backup of reviews, runs, settings and all project history. Choose the format The interface offers COCO, YOLO, semantic PNG masks, Pascal VOC, KITTI, detection CSV, CVAT for images, Label Studio tasks and folder-per-class outputs. Choose a format that can express the source task. YOLO task variants include detection, instance segmentation, pose and oriented boxes. Use COCO RLE or semantic PNGs for exact mask pixels. Polygon conversion can approximate masks. Draft source/confidence is preserved where the chosen format has room for it; recheck downstream behaviour rather than assuming every consumer reads those fields. Choose the media strategy Strategy Result Copy A separate image copy travels with the export Symbolic link Minimal extra storage; still depends on the original target path Hard link Shares bytes on the same filesystem; cannot cross drives Labels only Annotation files reference existing images; unavailable for layouts requiring images Moving linked exports to another machine can break them. A hard link also does not protect against external modification of the shared bytes. Choose copied media for an independent handoff. Python export import granum granum.export_yolo({"train": train_table, "val": valid_table}, "out/yolo", image_strategy="copy", task="detect") Here train_table and valid_table are the exact loaded revisions. YOLO export remaps class IDs to its contiguous class convention and excludes zero-weight rows. Inspect counts, class names, image hashes and a few difficult annotations after export. For full workspace recovery, use backup and restore .

title: Train a model
summary: Choose a dataset version and matching model task, record sample measurements, and inspect the completed run.
text: Runs → Train model starts a supervised model process using a named dataset version. The current catalogue includes detection, instance segmentation, pose, oriented detection, classification and semantic segmentation paths. See task support for dependencies and development qualification limits. Choose the data Select the dataset version, then its training and validation sets and, optionally, a held-out test set. If no versions are offered, create one from Images first. An exploratory version and an approved version have different review guarantees; read the acknowledgement or approval requirement shown. The task preflight checks the annotation contract, class maps, media and split overlap. Fix a mismatch before starting the model. Choosing detection simply because the intended mask task fails preflight would change what the experiment measures. Choose the model and recipe Choose the family, prediction task and size offered by the running build. Detection families include YOLO, RT-DETR and RF-DETR. YOLO also exposes mask, pose and rotated-box variants. The newer Torchvision paths use ResNet-18 for classification and LR-ASPP MobileNetV3 for semantic masks. Set epochs and the input-size controls supported by that family. Larger images and models can increase memory and processing time; check a short representative run before committing to a long schedule. RF-DETR has its own image-size behaviour. The model reference describes the catalogue without assuming one family is best for every dataset. Record per-sample metrics and predictions every epoch retains the observations used for learning analysis and supported Findings workflows. It adds inference work and storage; masks and embeddings can be substantially larger than scalar metrics. Collect the frequency your investigation needs. Compare with evaluates an earlier compatible model against the intended evaluation context. Only compare matching tasks. The full comparison guide explains the evidence needed before attributing a change to better data. Follow the job The progress card shows preparation, model loading, training, metric collection and evaluation phases. Inspect logs when progress stops or a dependency/device error appears. Closing the browser does not cancel a job. Supervised trainers can survive a service restart and reconnect; a dead trainer may instead be reported as interrupted. Use Cancel when you intend to stop. Inspect the resulting status and partial records before starting again. Conflicting model jobs can occupy the worker; the interface reports when a new request cannot start. Inspect the result Open the completed run and check its source version, class map, recipe, selected checkpoint and recorded metrics. Classification uses accuracy/loss, semantic segmentation uses pixel and class-overlap metrics, and detection-style tasks use their task-specific matching. These headline numbers are not interchangeable. Where a test set was supplied, keep its final evaluation separate from iterative validation decisions. Open several joined samples and inspect predictions against their actual labels before relying on a score. Continue with reading runs , learning and error inspection . A complete panoptic trainer and managed training/sweep scheduler are Not yet included . Newly added classification/semantic paths still require broader dataset, device and dashboard qualification.

title: Choose a training task
summary: Match dataset labels, model families and evaluation metrics before starting a training job.
text: Start from a named dataset version and choose the model family that matches its labels. The current development source includes the task paths below; each still needs compatible dependencies, readable media and matching class definitions across splits. Task map Task Current model path Main recorded measurement Object detection YOLO, RT-DETR, RF-DETR Detection precision, recall and average precision Instance segmentation YOLO segmentation variants Mask-based object matching Keypoints YOLO pose variants Keypoint similarity and per-landmark observations Oriented detection YOLO OBB variants Rotated-overlap matching Image classification Torchvision ResNet-18 Accuracy, loss and macro F1 Semantic segmentation Torchvision LR-ASPP MobileNetV3 Mean class IoU and pixel accuracy Classification and semantic training are newly implemented development paths. Full representative dataset/GPU/dashboard qualification is still in progress. Their model entries do not imply support for arbitrary classifiers or every semantic architecture. Start a job Open Datasets and select the frozen version to train on. Choose Train , the model family, task variant and model size available in your build. Confirm training, validation and any held-out test selection. Keep the test set outside routine tuning. Set epochs, image size and supported recipe controls. Enable per-sample recording when you need repeated observations and overlays. Read task-preflight errors before starting; fix the data rather than selecting an unrelated task. Start the run, inspect progress/logs, then check the stored measurements and checkpoint. Data requirements Task preflight checks readable media, compatible class maps, task geometry and split overlap. Classification needs one valid whole-image class per image. Semantic training needs class-ID masks with compatible ignore handling and labelled pixels. Both need at least two represented classes, including background where it is part of the semantic task. Mask resizing that removes all labelled pixels is an error; choose an appropriate resolution. Training weights affect the training population/sampling. Evaluation retains its declared population; inspect any exclusions before comparing scores. Semantic metrics aggregate class intersections/unions rather than simply averaging image means. Not yet included A complete panoptic trainer, dedicated YOLO classification callback, arbitrary architecture catalogue and managed hyperparameter sweeps are not yet included. Specialised evaluation screens can still be more limited than the underlying metric collector. Use the recorded run/table workspace and metrics guide for the exact outputs available.

title: Read a run
summary: Scores per round, the framework-neutral final score, and where each number comes from.
headings: From a run to the images
text: The Runs screen lists every run in the project with its model, the data versions it used, its rounds and its scores, best value marked. Click a row to open the run itself; the buttons on the right lead to its per-image views. The chart Rounds along the bottom, one line per run, metric chosen at the top left. Two shapes are worth recognising: A curve still climbing at the last round suggests investigating schedule length, convergence and noise. It does not guarantee that more epochs will produce a useful detector. Validation flattening while training loss keeps falling can indicate overfitting, but also inspect support, split differences and measurement noise. It does not prove that particular labels are wrong. Held-out evidence matters, especially when training-set findings become quiet. The columns Column What it is Status Running (with the round it is on), finished, cancelled or failed Model Family, weights and image size Train / validation / test data The exact set versions, so two rows can be compared honestly Epochs Rounds logged mAP50 , mAP50-95 , Precision , Recall The trainer's own metrics for the last round Test mAP50 The held-out score, when the run had a test set The trainer's metrics are useful for watching progress, but can differ from Granum's final checkpoint scoring and Evaluation of stored per-epoch predictions. Compare the same evaluator, label version, checkpoint definition, split and prediction/threshold policy. The dedicated comparison checks these boundaries; a metric name alone is not enough. The course results show an actual case where framework-history and final Granum mAP differ. → Runs and metrics From a run to the images Samples opens per-image learning: which images were learned early, late, unstably or never. Findings ranks individual labels worth checking. Compare puts this run beside the one before it. Opening a run gives the joined view: per-image metrics beside their recorded versioned input samples. Later working-label edits do not rewrite the historical measurement. Inspect the input version before interpreting a disagreement. A run that produced nothing A run cancelled before its first round finished has no metrics and no predictions, so the evidence screens have nothing to show and say so rather than displaying an empty chart. It still appears in the list, with its status, because it happened.

title: Per-image learning
summary: Which images the model learned early, late, unstably or never — and what to do with each group.
text: Samples , on a run that recorded per-image metrics every round, groups every image by how it behaved across the run. A single round says which images the model gets wrong now; the sequence says much more. The categories Category What happened What it usually means Early Learned quickly and stayed learned Ordinary, well-labelled images Mid Learned somewhere in the middle Ordinary Late Only learned near the end Hard examples, or labels that fight the convention Unstable Learned, then lost again, perhaps repeatedly Inconsistent labelling, or genuinely ambiguous content Not learned Never reached the threshold Where wrong labels concentrate — check these first Too few observations Seen in under three rounds, or in less than half the rounds other images were No verdict. Not a judgement about the image Empty No labels and no predictions Negatives, or images nobody labelled Speed is judged relative to this run, not at fixed epoch numbers: an image learned at round 5 is late in a run where most images are learned by round 2, and early in one where most take ten. Fixed cut-offs put nearly everything in one bucket for the short schedules people actually run. How to use it Not learned and Unstable are the two groups worth your attention. Sort by them, open a few, and you will usually find one of four things: a label that is wrong, a label your convention does not actually want, an object that is genuinely invisible at this resolution, or a hard case worth keeping. The first two are fixes. The third is a reason to raise the image size. The fourth is a reason to leave the label alone — and Granum expects that answer often enough that "keep" is a first-class decision everywhere. The image viewer Click any card to open it full screen. Beyond the usual zoom and pan: Key Action [ ] Step back and forward through the rounds Space Play the rounds as an animation L / G Show labels / show the model's boxes M Show only the mistakes K / R Keep the image / mark it for removal U Undo that decision F , + − Fit, zoom Watching the boxes move round by round is the quickest way to tell a hard example from a bad label: a hard example is found late and then held; a bad label is fought the whole way, or found confidently and then abandoned as the model learns the labelled version. The round strip marks the threshold and the rounds where the image dropped below it, so an unstable image shows its own history at a glance. Applying removals Images marked for removal are collected; applying them writes a new version of the set without them and records them in the dataset's removed set, where they can be put back. → Isolate, remove and restore Per-image F1 alone will not find every label error An image with one wrong box among thirty correct ones scores well all run and never appears in Not learned . That is exactly what Findings is for: it works at the level of the individual box rather than the image.

title: Work the Findings queue
summary: A ranked list of labels worth checking, the evidence for each, and a decision you record.
headings: What is judged, and what is not
text: Findings takes a finished run and produces a ranked queue of individual labels the model persistently disagreed with, each with the evidence behind it and a decision you record. It is the screen that turns "the model is worse than I expected" into an afternoon of specific, finite work. The four rules Rule What was seen What to do Missing label A confident prediction where nothing is labelled, round after round Add a box if the object should be labelled Wrong class A confident prediction of another class sitting on your label Change the class if your label is wrong Loose box A confident prediction of the right class overlapping your box, but not enough to match Tighten the box if it does not fit Not found A label the model never finds, with none of the above explaining why Check it; keep it if it is a valid hard case Rules are versioned. Every decision records which version of the rules raised the finding it answered, so when the rules change, old decisions still say what they were about. What is judged, and what is not Only rounds where the model was competent. The window starts at the first round where the set's recall reached 90% of its best. Before that the model misses everything, which says nothing about your labels. Only what recurs. A finding needs at least two rounds and at least a fifth of the judged window — half, for Not found , because a miss is weaker evidence than a confident prediction. Ranked by strength. The score is how often it was seen multiplied by how confident the model was. A confident wrong class seen in every round outranks a label missed in half of them. Held-out sets first The page opens on a held-out set — validation or test — because the evidence there is stronger. On the training set the model learns your labels as they are, including the wrong ones, so a genuine error often stops appearing in later rounds. The training tab shows a notice saying exactly that, and findings carry a note when the model stopped raising them ("last seen in round 7"). Working the queue Cards show a close-up crop around the finding with the label and the model's box drawn on it. Filter by rule and by whether you have decided. The progress bar estimates the work left at twenty seconds a finding — an estimate, and labelled as one. Click a card for the full-screen reviewer: Key Action ← → Previous / next image ↑ ↓ Move between the findings on this image Z Close-up or whole image C Label is right — checked, a valid hard case F Fix — records "fixing" and opens this image in the editor A Ambiguous — nobody can say what is right L Later — needs another look X Exclude image — should not be used for training U Undo the decision Decisions are appended to the dataset's review log with the rule, the strength of the evidence and the rules version. Reading the evidence honestly Each finding states what was seen in plain terms: "The model predicts person here in 9 of 11 rounds (confidence 0.62–0.88), and nothing is labelled here." That sentence is the whole claim. It is not a verdict that your label is wrong, and about a fifth of the time — more in unusual datasets — the right answer is Label is right . That is a feature. A queue that was always right would be a labelling model, and you would not need to look. → What the evidence is worth If the page is empty Three reasons, and the page says which: the run did not record predictions per round; the run was cancelled before it produced any; or the model never became competent on that set, so no round was judged. The third is common with short schedules on small datasets — train longer, then come back.

title: Compare two runs
summary: Improved, regressed, unchanged and unmatched images — and what the comparison is worth.
headings: 1. May these two be compared at all?
2. What may be read into it?
text: Compare runs puts a baseline and a candidate side by side on the evaluation set they share. Reach it from the Runs header, or from a run's Compare button, which compares it with the run before it. The page answers three questions in order, and the order is the point. 1. May these two be compared at all? Before any number is shown, Granum checks the pair and refuses rather than averaging when the comparison would be meaningless: Check Refuses when Warns when Evaluation set The two were scored on different sets — Evaluation version — The same set, but a different version: the labels changed Scoring rules The runs used different matching or operating points One did not record its policy Classes The class lists have nothing in common They differ but overlap Training recipe — Model, size, rounds or batch differ Seeds — One seed each: small differences cannot be separated from noise Warnings are listed above the numbers, with the passed checks collapsed behind a count. 2. What may be read into it? The verdict card names the comparison: Controlled — only the thing under test changed. Observational — the data changed too. "The comparison shows what happened alongside that change, not what any single edit caused." And the headline score, with a declared tolerance : a difference smaller than it is reported as too close to call , because with one seed per run nobody has measured the run-to-run spread. This is a declared threshold, not a measured noise level, and the page says so. 3. What actually moved? Five tiles count every image of the shared set: improved , regressed , unchanged , only in baseline , only in candidate . Click one to filter the table below it. Images are paired by image reference , never by row, so a version that removed images cannot misalign the comparison. Unchanged means the same true positives, misses and false positives — not merely a similar score. An image that traded a miss for a false positive did not stay the same. The unmatched tiles are listed, not dropped. When you removed 200 images between runs, that is the most important fact on the page. Below the table: pooled scores on the images both runs scored, with their support; slices by class and by object size, each marked too few to call under 30 labels; what changed in the data — images added, removed or edited, boxes drawn, deleted, relabelled or moved; and what it cost — rounds, training time, and the review decisions recorded between the two runs, with observed counts separate from the estimate. Download report Download report saves the whole comparison as JSON: the versions of everything, every check and its result, every image with its before and after counts, the slices, the data change and the costs. It is meant for the places a screenshot will not do — a pilot write-up, a regression record attached to a release, or a colleague who wants to check your arithmetic. Getting a comparison worth reading Change one thing at a time. If you fix labels and switch from nano to medium and add 5,000 images, the page will tell you honestly that it cannot attribute anything — which is correct, and not what you wanted to learn. Keep the evaluation set fixed across the comparison, and the honest version of the question stays answerable.

title: Record per sample metrics
summary: Link model measurements to exact input samples, splits and epochs so errors remain inspectable.
text: Aggregate metrics describe a run. Per-sample metrics explain which inputs produced that result. Granum stores these as metrics tables referencing the input table and its sample IDs. Choose a collector Task Collector or path Measurements Classification ClassificationMetricsCollector Prediction, confidence, loss and related classification measures Detection DetectionMetricsCollector(task="detect") Object matches and per-image precision, recall and F1 Instance segmentation DetectionMetricsCollector(task="segment") Matching based on mask IoU Pose DetectionMetricsCollector(task="pose") Matching based on OKS, with landmark properties Oriented boxes DetectionMetricsCollector(task="obb") Matching based on rotated IoU Semantic masks SemanticMetricsCollector Pixel accuracy and class intersections/unions/IoU Features or custom measures Embedding or functional collector Typed vectors or your own per-sample columns Attach observations to a run The following fragment assumes table , model and preprocess have been configured for your inputs: import granum from granum.metrics import ClassificationMetricsCollector, Predictor run = granum.init("inspection", "baseline", parameters={"seed": 7}) metrics = granum.collect_metrics( table, [ClassificationMetricsCollector(classes=["acceptable", "defect"])], predictor=Predictor(model, preprocess=preprocess), run=run, split="validation", constants={"epoch": 0}, ) print(metrics.join_input()[0]) run.set_status("finished") The class order must match the model output and table labels. Collect at each epoch if you need learning dynamics or recurring findings. Logging a single aggregate loss cannot reconstruct missing per-sample predictions later. Preserve identity The core collection pass traverses canonical table order. Each collector returns one value per input sample for every metric column. Framework adapters preserve explicit IDs through supported shuffle and subset operations. Do not attach arbitrary reordered predictions by positional guesswork. Keep the input version, split, epoch and evaluation settings with the measurements. Record the thresholds and task-specific geometry convention. Predictions should be in original-image coordinates; semantic masks should use the original resolution. Check the result Open the run, inspect several joined rows and compare predictions with their source images. Count collected samples and explain any intentional exclusions. Use custom metrics for a runnable model-free example and run comparison before comparing experiments.

title: Examples and complete workflows
summary: Choose a runnable Granum example or find the reserved place for a future model and dataset recipe.
headings: Build a workflow from supported pieces
text: Use the guided course for a complete dashboard workflow. Use the Python examples when integrating an existing pipeline. Each recipe has its own dataset, model and optional dependency requirements; inspect them before running a download or starting training. Included examples The following files live in the repository's examples directory. Run them from the project checkout with Granum installed in the active environment. Read the file's inputs and output-root settings first. File What it demonstrates 01_tables_and_revisions.py Create data and preserve revisions 02_runs_and_metrics.py Record runs and sample measurements 03_label_error_ranking.py Rank candidates for label inspection 04_object_service.py Serve registered data 05_cifar10_resnet.py A concrete classification training loop 06_retrain_on_latest.py Consume revised data in another experiment 07_detection_yolo.py Object detection with YOLO 08_aerial_pipeline.py The aerial-data workflow The 12-step aerial course covers import, exploration, baseline training, review, candidate training, results, comparison, handoff and backup with recorded evidence. It remains a small example, not a capacity or accuracy promise for another dataset. Build a workflow from supported pieces For COCO/YOLO detection, masks, pose and OBBs, begin with formats , inspect/edit labels, freeze a version , then connect the corresponding training adapter . For custom tabular samples, use TableWriter and custom metrics . To add image measurements such as brightness, compute one value per canonical input row and create a typed column with add_column . Per-object measurements need a declared instance property. Embedding collection and shared projections are covered in embedding exploration . Reserved example recipes These recipes are Not yet included as complete Granum examples. Related primitives may already work; a reserved recipe still needs its own data preparation, executable training/evaluation path and expected-result checks.
